title: Where Have All the Isms Gone?: On the Evolution of Knowledge
description: The roundtable examines how intellectual movements and paradigms have historically organized knowledge within disciplines -- from functionalism and structuralism in anthropology to postmodernism in various fields. The discussion explores whether contemporary scholarship has entered a phase where traditional movement categories no longer effectively structure academic thought. Key topics include Thomas Kuhn's paradigm shift theory, the Internet's fragmentation of knowledge dissemination, social polarization creating isolated communities of belief, and AI's generation of authentic and fabricated scholarly content. The organizers suggest we may be entering a new era in how knowledge is transmitted and organized across sciences and humanities.

title: Come Out Wherever You Are: In Search of Consciousness

The third approach, 4E Cognition (extended, embedded, embodied, enacted), proposes minds exist as "a dynamic amalgam of the world, our bodies, and our brains," extending beyond brain-centered models.

title: Metaphysics
description: Physics examines Nature's fundamental properties; metaphysics investigates what must necessarily follow from those properties. For centuries, metaphysics provided the organizing framework for scientific research. However, 20th-century challenges emerged: quantum theory's Copenhagen interpretation emphasized epistemology over ontology, the "linguistic turn" discouraged claims beyond language's limits, and cognitive psychology shifted focus toward modes of cognition rather than Nature itself. Today, metaphysics experiences revival with refined understanding of empirical access to Nature. "Experimental metaphysics" now bridges quantum physics and metaphysical frameworks, while perceptual neuroscience analyzes ambiguous stimuli to inform consciousness studies. This roundtable examined how divergent perspectives -- sometimes paradoxical -- might be reconciled through metaphysics addressing these challenges.

title: Panacea or Poison: Placebos and Nocebos in Modern Medicine
description: The roundtable explores how placebos "work" for medical conditions despite being inert substances. It examines the mind-body connection, asking: "what is the work they do?" The discussion covers how beliefs about medications can affect biology similarly to active drugs, the inverse nocebo effect (where negative expectations produce symptoms), and the mechanisms linking thought to physical health outcomes. Historical context traces placebo effects to shamanic practices, while raising ethical questions about modern clinical applications.

title: Populism
description: Populism involves "political mobilization of 'the people' against a perceived elite caste of professional politicians." The roundtable explores what triggers such mass movements, examining whether Federalist Paper safeguards remain effective. Discussion covers perceived ruling-class failures, right vs. left-wing populism, and factors like nationalism, classism, religion, xenophobia, and domestic oppression. The page also examines whether anomie, alienation, social humiliation, and social media catalyze these movements globally.

description: Memory functions as "a dynamic process, a stream of renditions and reflections" rather than static storage. The event explores how memory "conveys to us not what strictly happened, but embeds us in a retained internal moment." Key themes include implicit versus explicit memories, memory's paradoxical nature (private yet collective), and its role in identity and consciousness.

title: Ethics & AI
description: The roundtable explored how artificial intelligence challenges traditional notions of justice and anonymity. Drawing on John Rawls's "veil of ignorance" thought experiment, the discussion examined how AI's collection of personal data -- behavioral patterns, vocal characteristics, word frequencies -- creates detailed cyber-profiles that strip away anonymity. The conversation addressed how machine learning algorithms are deployed in medical, legal, mortgage, and sentencing contexts, often making predictions about individuals without their input. Key concerns included whether AI serves human interests and the ethical implications of algorithmic categorization affecting resource distribution and social opportunity.

title: How Deep Do We Go? Behavior, Mind, and The 4-Billion-Year History of Life
description: This roundtable examined Joseph LeDoux's book The Deep History of Ourselves: The Four-Billion-Year Story of How We Got Conscious Brains. The core premise challenges conventional understanding of human emotions as evolutionarily pre-formed states. LeDoux argues that single-cell microbes possessed basic survival mechanisms (detecting danger, seeking nutrients, maintaining fluid balance, reproduction) whose modern manifestations we interpret as fear, hunger, thirst, and pleasure. He contends emotions result from cognitive interpretation of significant life moments and require our specific brain architecture.

title: Emergence of Empathy: Encountering The Other Through Fiction
description: The event explores how empathy -- derived from Greek "pathos" meaning "to endure" -- functions through fiction. Coined in 1909 by psychologist Edward Bradford Titchner as a translation of German "Einfuhlung," empathy represents an emotional strategy to "feel into" others and resolve internal conflicts. The roundtable examines how fictional narratives shape our understanding of intimate human experiences including love, death, friendship, loss, and fear through imaginary characters we encounter in beloved books.

speakerDetails.name: Hava Tirosh-Samuelson, Ph.D.
speakerDetails.role: Regents' Professor; Irving and Miriam Lowe Professor of Modern Judaism; Director of Jewish Studies; Professor of History, Arizona State University
speakerDetails.bio: Focus: Jewish intellectual history, religion and science, religious environmentalism.

title: Mind Matters: Past, Present, and Future
description: The roundtable traces humanity's evolving understanding of mind from ancient philosophy through contemporary science. Beginning with "Xenophanes' 6th c. BCE theory of divine intellection imbuing, comprehending, and organizing the cosmos" through modern cognitive science, panelists explore how advances in brain science, computer science, mathematics, physics, and psychology have shaped our conception of mind. The discussion examines whether metaphysics and theology should inform future understanding of consciousness.

speakerDetails.name: John Krakauer
speakerDetails.role: John C. Malone Professor, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine; Director of Brain, Learning, Animation, and Movement Lab; Co-founder of Kata Project

speakerDetails.name: Jonathan Kramnick
speakerDetails.role: Maynard Mack Professor of English, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in 18th-century literature and cognitive science.

speakerDetails.name: George Makari
speakerDetails.role: Director, DeWitt Wallace Institute for Psychiatry History; Professor of Psychiatry, Weill-Cornell Medical College
speakerDetails.bio: Historian and psychoanalyst.

speakerDetails.name: Kenneth Miller
speakerDetails.role: Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience, Columbia University; Co-Director, Center for Theoretical Neuroscience

speakerDetails.name: Barbara Montero
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, University of Notre Dame
speakerDetails.bio: Researches embodiment and consciousness.

title: Science, Art & Society 2
description: The roundtable examined how postmodernism damaged both art and science by "casting out beauty from art and validity of facts from science," resulting in public disconnection and reduced funding. The discussion addressed bridging gaps between these disciplines and society, improving literacy, and achieving cultural respect for both fields.

title: Science, Art & Society 1
description: The roundtable addressed "the multi-directional relationship between science, art, and society" which requires repair. The organizers noted that postmodernism has harmed both disciplines by "casting out of beauty from art and validity of facts from science," resulting in public disconnection reflected in inadequate arts funding and poor science literacy. Key discussion questions included how to bridge gaps between art, science, and society; responsibilities of cultural and intellectual authorities; improving science and art literacy; repairing art's reputation post-postmodernism; and creating a culture valuing science and art funding.

title: STEAM & the Future of Education 1
description: The roundtable addressed "Science Technology Engineering Art Mathematics" as an emerging educational movement. STEAM "advocates for the integration of arts and design learning in STEM," originating in 2008 to promote well-rounded thinking and cross-disciplinary innovation. Key discussion topics included successful STEAM teaching methods, curriculum design, implementation within existing educational systems, challenges faced, and preparation for 21st-century education.

title: Science-Art Collaboration 2
description: The event explores "collaboration between the arts and sciences" with historical context from the Renaissance through modern initiatives. Key discussion topics include: defining collaboration, funding mechanisms, authorship questions, and whether art influences science as science influences art.

title: STEAM & the Future of Education 2
description: The event explores "STEAM -- or Science Technology Engineering Art Mathematics" as an educational movement that "advocates for the integration of arts and design learning in STEM." Key topics address successful STEAM teaching methods, curriculum design, implementation challenges, and "new educational models for transdisciplinary work."

title: Science-Art Collaboration 1
description: The roundtable explored artistic and scientific collaboration, noting its "rich history dating back to the Renaissance" with a resurgence in the 1960s through groups like Experiments in Art & Technology. The event addressed key questions about interdisciplinary work: What defines collaboration? How does funding work? Who owns collaborative products? Can art influence science as much as science influences art?

title: American Poetry Today
description: The roundtable explores contemporary poetry through multiple perspectives. Opening with quotes from modernist poets Ezra Pound and William Carlos Williams about poetry's significance, the discussion addresses which contemporary poets merit attention, what inspires them, and why this art form matters in an age of "sociopolitical turmoil, Internet overload, media saturation." The program featured "a roundtable of diverse and accomplished poets" examining poetry's appeal across conceptual, musical, visual, literary, sociopolitical, and psychological dimensions, followed by Q&A.

speakerDetails.name: Patricia Carlin
speakerDetails.role: Ph.D. from Princeton (Shakespeare studies, poetics)
speakerDetails.bio: Recent collection: Second Nature (May 2017). Other works: Quantum Jitters, Original Green, Shakespeare's Mortal Men.

speakerDetails.name: Amy Holman
speakerDetails.role: Pushcart Prize-nominated poet and literary consultant
speakerDetails.bio: Collection: Wrens Fly Through This Opened Window. Published four poetry chapbooks including prize-winning Wait For Me, I'm Gone.

speakerDetails.name: Paolo Javier
speakerDetails.role: Featured artist in MoMA PS1's 2015 Greater NY Show
speakerDetails.bio: Four full-length poetry collections including Court of the Dragon (Nightboat Books 2015). Collaboration: Ur'lyeh/Aklopolis (2017).

speakerDetails.name: Stephen Massimilla
speakerDetails.role: Poet, scholar, professor, painter
speakerDetails.bio: M.F.A. and Ph.D. from Columbia University. Multi-genre volume: Cooking with the Muse (Tupelo, 2016) - won Eric Hoffer Book Award and National Indie Excellence Award.

title: "Fake" Knowledge: Knowing and the Illusion of Knowing
description: The event explores how humans have always relied on distributed knowledge through social contracts. It examines mass delusions and our collective intuition, questioning what we should believe versus what remains unverifiable. The roundtable addresses how internet technology -- as an "impersonal cloud-mind" -- changes our ability to distinguish internal from external knowledge and whether it creates an illusion of understanding. Key questions include whether collective knowledge transcends individual limitations, whether more information necessarily produces wisdom, and whether we're moving toward a human-machine partnership previously confined to science fiction.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Boghossian
speakerDetails.role: Silver Professor of Philosophy, NYU; Director, Global Institute for Advanced Study
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from Princeton (Philosophy), B.Sc. from Trent (Physics). Elected to American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2012). Research focuses on epistemology and philosophy.

speakerDetails.name: Daniel Kahneman
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Renowned for joint research with Amos Tversky on human judgment. Nobel Prize in Economics (2002), Presidential Medal of Freedom (2013).

speakerDetails.name: Eric Kandel
speakerDetails.role: University Professor, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Kavli Professor; Director of Kavli Institute for Brain Science; Co-Director of Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute; Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator. Harvard College and NYU School of Medicine graduate.

speakerDetails.name: Mark Mitton
speakerDetails.role: Magician
speakerDetails.bio: Uses magic to understand perception and cognition, specializing in physical misdirection and "embodied cognition." Presents on perception and deception globally.

speakerDetails.name: Daphna Shohamy
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Psychology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Works at Mind, Brain Behavior Institute and Kavli Institute. Research combines brain imaging with patient studies to understand how expectations shape memories.

speakerDetails.name: Steven Sloman
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic and Psychological Sciences, Brown University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from Stanford (1990), postdoctoral research at University of Michigan. Editor-in-Chief of Cognition journal.

title: Complexity and Emergence II: Visions of Cosmic Order, from Particles to People
description: The roundtable explores "what principles of order underlie the ascent of complexity, from the simplest particles of physics heralding the birth of the universe, through biological forms, to the achievements of civilization." It investigates whether "combination and integration led to multiple fundamental levels from quarks to culture" and examines the creative processes underlying cosmic order and human consciousness.

speakerDetails.name: William Grassie
speakerDetails.role: Interdisciplinary scholar
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. in political science from Middlebury College and Ph.D. in Religion from Temple University; focused on nuclear disarmament, citizen diplomacy, and sustainability.

speakerDetails.name: David Grinspoon
speakerDetails.role: Astrobiologist and prize-winning author; Senior Scientist, Planetary Science Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Researches climate evolution and conditions for life elsewhere.

speakerDetails.name: Tim Maudlin
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. in Physics and Philosophy from Yale; Ph.D. in History and Philosophy of Science from University of Pittsburgh.

speakerDetails.name: Ilya Temkin
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Biology, Northern Virginia Community College; Research Associate, Smithsonian Institution
speakerDetails.bio: Expert on bivalve mollusks and evolution.

speakerDetails.name: Tyler Volk
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Biology and Environmental Studies, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "Quarks to Culture: How We Came to Be" (Columbia University Press, May 2017).

title: Design in Nature
description: The roundtable examines how natural design relates to historical concepts of teleology and divinity. It explores whether Darwinian adaptationism can reframe immanence in terms of physical principles underlying functional design in nature. The event opens with a Leonardo da Vinci quote about nature's superior design elegance.

speakerDetails.name: Elizabeth Alter
speakerDetails.role: Evolutionary geneticist; Professor of Biology, City University of New York (Graduate Center and York College); Research Associate, American Museum of Natural History
speakerDetails.bio: Studies aquatic biodiversity generation in extreme environments.

speakerDetails.name: Adrian Bejan
speakerDetails.role: J.A. Jones Distinguished Professor, Duke University
speakerDetails.bio: Researches applied physics, thermodynamics, and the Constructal Law. Author of 30+ books and 600+ peer-reviewed articles.

speakerDetails.name: Robin Collins
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of Philosophy, Messiah College
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from University of Notre Dame (1993); graduate training in theoretical physics from University of Texas at Austin. 45+ substantial publications in philosophy.

speakerDetails.name: Mark A. Norell
speakerDetails.role: Chairman of Department of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History
speakerDetails.bio: Born July 26, 1957. BS from Long Beach State (1980); MS from San Diego State (1983).

speakerDetails.name: Caleb Scharf
speakerDetails.role: Director of Astrobiology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Researches cosmology, exoplanetary science, and astrobiology. Global Science Coordinator for Earth-Life Science Institute's Origins Network.

title: Music to Whose Ears III: Music and Healing
description: The roundtable explored therapeutic applications of melody and rhythm for cognitive and motor conditions including non-fluent aphasia, autism, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. It addressed how music alleviates pain and anxiety in preterm infants and surgical patients. Research indicates musically trained children show enhanced memory performance correlated with IQ, and musical training may slow cognitive decline in normal aging. The discussion examined "possible mechanisms of music's beneficial influence on the brain."

speakerDetails.name: Evelina Fedorenko
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Director of the EvLab at Harvard Medical School/Mass General Hospital
speakerDetails.bio: Cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the human language system.

speakerDetails.name: Marina Korsakova-Kreyn
speakerDetails.role: Professional pianist and scholar in music perception and cognition
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from University of Texas at Dallas, researching emotional responses to music.

speakerDetails.name: Andrea Norton
speakerDetails.role: Classically-trained singer and choral conductor
speakerDetails.bio: Degree from Westminster Choir College; experienced in community music programs.

speakerDetails.name: Andrew Rossetti
speakerDetails.role: Clinical music psychotherapist and researcher
speakerDetails.bio: Coordinating multi-site music therapy programs at Mount Sinai Beth Israel Medical Center.

speakerDetails.name: John Schaefer
speakerDetails.role: Host and producer of WNYC's "New Sounds" (founded 1982) and "Soundcheck" podcast

speakerDetails.name: Concetta Tomaino
speakerDetails.role: Executive Director and co-founder of the Institute for Music and Neurologic Function

title: The Displaced and The Other
description: The roundtable explores human migration across generations and borders. As noted, "with more than 65 million refugees and displaced persons around the globe," the discussion examines how societies respond to displacement through "creativity and compassion rather than detachment and fear."

speakerDetails.name: Lisa DeBenedittis
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Design Research at Parsons School of Design; former Vice Provost of The New School
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from NYU (2005) in aesthetics of subjectivity; trained analyst at Jungian Psychoanalytic Association.

speakerDetails.name: Simon Deng
speakerDetails.role: Human rights activist from Sudan's Shilluk Kingdom
speakerDetails.bio: Escaped childhood slavery and obtained U.S. asylum and citizenship. Founded Sudan Freedom initiatives.

speakerDetails.name: Uri Hasson
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Department of Psychology and Neuroscience Institute, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Grew up in Jerusalem; Ph.D. in Neurobiology from Weizmann Institute; postdoctoral fellow at NYU.

speakerDetails.name: Athena Viscusi
speakerDetails.role: Psychosocial Care Specialist at MSF/Doctors Without Borders USA
speakerDetails.bio: Former Mental Health Officer directing programs in Haiti, South Sudan, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Myanmar, and Palestine.

speakerDetails.name: Morris Vogel
speakerDetails.role: President, Tenement Museum (since 2008)
speakerDetails.bio: American social and urban historian; Ph.D. from University of Chicago (1974); former Temple University professor.

title: Pain
description: The roundtable explores pain as both a biological and subjective phenomenon. Opening with an Aeschylus quote about suffering and wisdom, it examines pain's role in homeostasis, current scientific understanding, pain management approaches, analgesics (particularly opioids), and ethical considerations in pain research involving humans and other species.

speakerDetails.name: Apkar Apkarian
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Physiology, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Focuses on brain mechanisms underlying chronic back pain with 50+ publications and ongoing clinical trials.

speakerDetails.name: Inna Belfer
speakerDetails.role: Health Scientist Administrator/Project Officer, Office of Research on Women's Health
speakerDetails.bio: Expert in human pain genetics and clinical pain assessment; neurologist with neurobiology and human genetics training.

speakerDetails.name: Anis Dizdarevic
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Clinical Professor of Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine, Columbia University Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in acute/chronic pain management and pain prevention.

speakerDetails.name: Allen Fein
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Department of Cell Biology, UConn Health
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins; former Director of Marine Biological Laboratory's Sensory Physiology division.

speakerDetails.name: Rebecca Seal
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Departments of Neurobiology and Otolaryngology, University of Pittsburgh Center for Pain Research
speakerDetails.bio: Studies neurotransmitter transporters and nervous system function.

title: The Library as Reality and Metaphor
description: The event explored libraries across multiple dimensions -- physical, digital, representational -- and their epistemic, organizational, and memory functions. The roundtable opened with a Jorge Luis Borges quotation about "the vast, contradictory Library" as metaphor for human imagination and knowledge construction.

speakerDetails.name: Daniel Goroff
speakerDetails.role: Vice President and Program Director, Alfred P. Sloan Foundation; Professor Emeritus of Mathematics and Economics, Harvey Mudd College

speakerDetails.name: Anthony Grafton
speakerDetails.role: Professor of European History, Princeton University (since 1975)
speakerDetails.bio: Visiting professor at College de France, the Louvre, and other institutions.

speakerDetails.name: Carol Mandel
speakerDetails.role: Dean, NYU Division of Libraries
speakerDetails.bio: Leader in research librarianship during digital transformation.

speakerDetails.name: Alberto Manguel
speakerDetails.role: Argentinian-Canadian writer, translator, and critic
speakerDetails.bio: Former director of Argentine National Library; Formentor Prize 2017 recipient.

speakerDetails.name: Ken Soehner
speakerDetails.role: Arthur K. Watson Chief Librarian, Thomas J. Watson Library, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Autism and the Mind/Brain
description: This roundtable explored how autism, a neurodevelopmental disorder affecting over 1% of the population, was historically misunderstood as resulting from poor parental relationships. The event examined current scientific evidence demonstrating that autism results from abnormalities in brain development, and that the behavior observed in children is the consequence of disturbances in brain circuitry. Participants discussed the diagnosis history, current treatment approaches, and how advances in understanding the mind-brain relationship have shaped modern perspectives.

speakerDetails.name: Andrew Gerber
speakerDetails.role: Medical Director/CEO, Austen Riggs Center; Associate Clinical Professor, Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Columbia University Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in Psychology from Anna Freud Centre and University College London.

speakerDetails.name: Nouchine Hadjikhani
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor in Radiology, Harvard Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: MD, PhD; directs Neurolimbic research laboratory at Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging in Boston. Research focus includes visual system, migraine, and emotion.

speakerDetails.name: Craig Newschaffer
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Drexel University School of Public Health
speakerDetails.bio: Founding director of A.J. Drexel Autism Institute; Vice President of International Society for Autism Research.

speakerDetails.name: Jeremy Veenstra-VanderWeele
speakerDetails.role: Mortimer D. Sackler, M.D. Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Child and adolescent psychiatrist specializing in molecular and translational neuroscience research for autism spectrum disorder treatments.

speakerDetails.name: Martha Welch
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Columbia University Medical Center (Departments of Pediatrics and Pathology & Cell Biology)
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Nurture Science Program in Pediatrics and BrainGut Initiative in Developmental Neuroscience.

title: Embodied AI
description: The event explores how physical embodiment enhances artificial intelligence cognition. The core concept involves deploying natural language processing platforms -- like IBM Watson -- with sensory capabilities (eyes, ears, touch) and physical actuators (hands, feet, face) into real-world environments. This approach bridges classical AI's mind-body dualism and enables human augmentation across healthcare, supply chain management, and operational domains.

speakerDetails.name: Michael Bess
speakerDetails.role: Chancellor's Professor of History, Vanderbilt University
speakerDetails.bio: Specialist in 20th-21st century Europe with focus on interactions between social and cultural processes and technological change.

speakerDetails.name: Ned Block
speakerDetails.role: Silver Professor of Philosophy, Psychology, and Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Works in philosophy of mind and cognitive science foundations; Fellow of the American Academy.

speakerDetails.name: David Hanson
speakerDetails.role: Founder and CEO, Hanson Robotics Lab
speakerDetails.bio: Creates humanlike, expressive robots with remarkable expressiveness, aesthetics and interactivity.

speakerDetails.name: Jeffrey Kephart
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished RSM, Symbiotic Cognitive Systems; IEEE Fellow; IBM Academy of Technology Member
speakerDetails.bio: IBM Research scientist specializing in computer virus epidemiology and immune systems and embodied cognition co-strategist.

speakerDetails.name: Francesca Rossi
speakerDetails.role: IBM Fellow & IBM AI Ethics Global Leader
speakerDetails.bio: Based at T.J. Watson IBM Research Lab; leads AI ethics initiatives.

title: Coding and the New Human Phenotype (Weekend Conference Overview)
description: The event explores how life operates as "articulation of code" from DNA to phenotype. It examines digital coding's pervasive role in modern experience -- from cryptocurrency to surveillance -- and questions what may be lost through encoding phenomena. The conference investigates "the digitalization of life and the growing metaverse" potentially separating humans from direct, unmediated experience, while examining benefits and dangers.

title: The Electorate: 2016
status: Past Event -- Cocktail Benefit Reception and Roundtable
description: The organization hosted a cocktail reception and roundtable benefit in memory of Themis and Theodore Dimon featuring discussions on the 2016 electorate.

title: Happiness
description: The roundtable explores happiness across philosophical and psychological dimensions. It examines whether contentment solely defines a flourishing life, whether pleasure's value lies in the experience itself or in one's perception of it, and how individual happiness relates to others' welfare. Key questions address whether certain pleasures hold greater worth and if happiness is essential for living well. The discussion considers positive psychology's role in defining and measuring happiness, and its impact on socioeconomic theories and policies.

speakerDetails.name: Alberto Bisin
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Economics, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Elected Fellow of the Econometric Society; fellow of NBER, Center for Experimental Social Sciences at NYU, IGIER at Bocconi, CIREQ at University of Montreal, IZA at University of Bonn.

speakerDetails.name: Shimon Edelman
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, Cornell University
speakerDetails.bio: Holds degrees in electrical engineering and computer science; teaches behavioral, neural, evolutionary, and computational aspects of mind and behavior.

speakerDetails.name: Benjamin Radcliff
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Political Science, University of Notre Dame
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on how human happiness is politically produced and distributed; published in American Political Science Review, Journal of Politics, Perspectives on Politics.

speakerDetails.name: Wendy Suzuki
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neural Science and Psychology, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Neuroscience from UC San Diego; completed postdoctoral fellowship at National Institutes of Health; faculty at NYU's Center for Neural Science.

speakerDetails.name: Christine Vitrano
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Philosophy, Brooklyn College, CUNY
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "The Nature and Value of Happiness"; co-author with Steven M. Cahn of "Happiness and Goodness: Philosophical Reflections on Living Well."

title: Creative Turbulence Art Exhibition
description: This exhibition merged art and science by pairing artists with physicists to create four collaborative artworks exploring fluid dynamics, turbulence, and complex systems. The curator noted that "fluids are a part of everyone's daily life -- from stirring coffee to flying in various conditions" making the work relatable.

title: Fear: Wherefore, Whence?
description: The roundtable explores the nature of fear and anxiety across multiple dimensions. Opening with classical quotes from Sophocles and Leviticus, it examines neurobiological, physiological, behavioral, and cognitive factors in fear responses. The discussion considers whether human fear experiences differ fundamentally from those of other animals, and whether anxiety represents a central node connecting fundamental aspects of mental existence, as Freud theorized.

speakerDetails.name: Nouchine Hadjikhani, MD, PhD
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor in Radiology, Harvard Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: Directs the Neurolimbic research laboratory at Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging in Boston; invited Professor at Gillberg Neuropsychiatric Center, Gothenburg, Sweden. Research spans visual system, migraine, and emotion studies.

speakerDetails.name: Robert Kurzban, PhD
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, University of Pennsylvania
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from UC Santa Barbara's Center for Evolutionary Psychology (1998); postdoctoral training at Caltech, UCLA Anthropology, and University of Arizona.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph LeDoux, PhD
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on emotion, memory, consciousness and their brain interactions. Elected to National Academy of Sciences and American Academy of Arts and Sciences; recipient of numerous awards.

speakerDetails.name: Francis Lee, MD, PhD
speakerDetails.role: Mortimer D. Sackler Professor & Vice Chair for Research, Department of Psychiatry, Weill-Cornell Medical College
speakerDetails.bio: Attending psychiatrist at New York-Presbyterian Hospital; MD and PhD from University of Michigan; psychiatry training at Payne Whitney Clinic.

speakerDetails.name: Eric R. Marcus, MD
speakerDetails.role: Director, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research; Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons
speakerDetails.bio: Training and supervising analyst; former president of New York County district branch, American Psychiatric Association.

title: Understanding Genius II: Women
description: The roundtable explores why naming five female geniuses proves difficult despite history's abundance of brilliant women. It examines how genius has been historically conceived and investigates how gender, institutions, and beliefs shaped the prospects of women of intelligence and insight.

speakerDetails.name: Joyce Chaplin
speakerDetails.role: James Duncan Phillips Professor of Early American History, Harvard University
speakerDetails.bio: Holds BA from Northwestern; MA and PhD from Johns Hopkins. Fulbright Scholar (1985-86) at University of Cambridge. Director of Harvard's American Studies program.

speakerDetails.name: Kathleen Kete
speakerDetails.role: Borden W. Painter, Jr., '58/H'95 Professor of European History, Trinity College
speakerDetails.bio: Secretary of the Faculty at Trinity College, CT. PhD in History from Harvard (1989); studied at Institut d'etudes politiques de Paris.

speakerDetails.name: Anne-Marie Levine
speakerDetails.role: Poet and Visual Artist
speakerDetails.bio: NYC-based poet and visual artist; former concert pianist. Author of three poetry collections: Euphorbia, Bus Ride to a Blue Movie, Oral History; forthcoming artists book: Reculer Pour Mieux Sauter.

speakerDetails.name: Darrin McMahon
speakerDetails.role: Mary Brinsmead Wheelock Professor of History, Dartmouth College
speakerDetails.bio: Formerly Ben Weider Professor at Florida State University (2004-2014). PhD from Yale (1998); educated at UC Berkeley.

speakerDetails.name: Susan Seymour
speakerDetails.role: Jean M. Pitzer Professor Emerita of Anthropology, Pitzer College
speakerDetails.bio: Former Vice President for Academic Affairs and Dean of Faculty. Coordinator of Women's Studies for Claremont Colleges. Research focuses on family and gender systems in India.

title: The Meditative State
description: The roundtable explores what constitutes meditation and examines the respective roles of conscious and unconscious processes in this voluntarily invoked mental state. It investigates how meditation differs from trance and hypnotic states, and examines neuroscientific data on how the brain alters its own functioning through meditative practice.

speakerDetails.name: Sara Lazar
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor in Psychology, Harvard Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: Associate Researcher in the Psychiatry Department at Massachusetts General Hospital. Her research focuses on neural mechanisms underlying benefits of yoga and meditation in clinical and healthy populations.

speakerDetails.name: Peter Malinowski
speakerDetails.role: Senior Lecturer in Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience, Liverpool John Moores University
speakerDetails.bio: Founding director of the Meditation and Mindfulness Research Group at Liverpool John Moores. Combines cognitive neuroscience expertise with extensive meditation practice and teaching experience.

speakerDetails.name: Koshin Paley Ellison
speakerDetails.role: Co-Founder of the New York Zen Center for Contemplative Care
speakerDetails.bio: Rev. Dr. with credentials in MFA, LMSW, DMIN. First Zen-based organization to offer fully accredited ACPE clinical chaplaincy training in America.

speakerDetails.name: Morgan Stebbins
speakerDetails.role: Supervising Analyst, Jungian Psychoanalytic Association in New York
speakerDetails.bio: Faculty member and Director of Training; teaches Religious Studies and Hermeneutics at New York Theological Seminary; began Zen training in San Francisco.

speakerDetails.name: Yi-Yuan Tang
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychological Sciences, Texas Tech University
speakerDetails.bio: Presidential Endowed Chair in Neuroscience and founding Director of Texas Tech Neuroimaging Institute. Fellow of Association for Psychological Sciences.

title: Genes, Computers, and Medicine
description: The roundtable explored how developments in computational neuroscience, molecular biology, and genomics have opened up new ways of looking at disease. The discussion examined potential innovations in understanding diseases and therapeutics, with particular focus on mental health disorders and etiology investigation.

speakerDetails.name: James Dahlman
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Biomedical Engineering, Georgia Tech
speakerDetails.bio: Chemical/bioengineer specializing in nanotechnology, genomics, and gene editing. PhD from MIT and Harvard Medical School (2014), studied RNA delivery and gene therapies with Robert Langer and Daniel Anderson.

speakerDetails.name: Francis Lee
speakerDetails.role: Mortimer D. Sackler Professor & Vice Chair for Research, Department of Psychiatry, Weill-Cornell Medical College
speakerDetails.bio: MD and PhD from University of Michigan; psychiatry training at Payne Whitney Clinic; attending psychiatrist at New York-Presbyterian Hospital.

speakerDetails.name: Karen Maschke
speakerDetails.role: Research Scholar, The Hastings Center
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in political science (Johns Hopkins), Master's in bioethics (Case Western Reserve University); Bioethics Fellow at Cleveland Clinic.

speakerDetails.name: Hans-Guido Wendel
speakerDetails.role: Principal Investigator, Cancer Genetics Laboratory, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center
speakerDetails.bio: MD trained in medicine in Aachen and Edinburgh; identifies new cancer therapies based on genetic disease origins.

title: Translation Matters
description: The roundtable explores why translation has evolved from a set of restricted technical procedures into the basis of all human culture. It examines translation as a psychic, aesthetic, and cultural phenomenon, addressing questions about the principle of displacement and exchange, political power, and linguistic capital. The event features celebrated literary translators and theorists working across different languages, genres, and periods.

speakerDetails.name: David Bellos
speakerDetails.role: Professor of French and Comparative Literature, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Studied Modern Languages at Oxford; taught at Edinburgh, Southampton, and Manchester universities before Princeton, where he directs the Program in Translation and Intercultural Communication. Author of books on Romain Gary and Jacques Tati.

speakerDetails.name: Bella Brodzki
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Comparative Literature, Sarah Lawrence College
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches world literature, translation studies, autobiography, and literary theory. Coeditor of Life/lines and author of "Can These Bones Live?: Translation, Survival..."

speakerDetails.name: Anne-Marie Levine
speakerDetails.role: Poet and Visual Artist
speakerDetails.bio: NYC-based poet and visual artist; former concert pianist. Author of three poetry collections: Euphorbia, Bus Ride to a Blue Movie, and Oral History, plus forthcoming artists' book.

speakerDetails.name: Suzanne Jill Levine
speakerDetails.role: Director of Translation Studies, University of California, Santa Barbara
speakerDetails.bio: Translator of Latin American authors including Borges, Cortazar, and Puig. Editor of Penguin Borges editions; 2014 Lambda Prize winner.

speakerDetails.name: Mark Polizzotti
speakerDetails.role: Author & Translator; Director of Publications Program, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
speakerDetails.bio: Author of Revolution of the Mind, Highway 61 Revisited, and Sympathy for the Traitor: A Translation Manifesto.

speakerDetails.name: Michelle Woods
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of English, SUNY New Paltz
speakerDetails.bio: Author of Kafka Translated, Censoring Translation, and Translating Milan Kundera; currently editing Authorizing Translation.

title: Speak, Memory
description: The roundtable explored advances in memory research over three decades, including neural processes of consolidation and reconsolidation, and the biochemistry of memory. Key questions addressed how research illuminates memory's role in development, treatment of memory impairment in aging populations, and dialogue between neuroscientists and memory scholars.

speakerDetails.name: Cristina Alberini
speakerDetails.role: Professor in the Center for Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Has studied biological mechanisms of long-term memory for 20 years, focusing on memory consolidation and reconsolidation, the processes by which newly learned information become long-lasting memories.

speakerDetails.name: Sven Bernecker
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, University of California, Irvine
speakerDetails.bio: Holds doctorate from Stanford University; recipient of Humboldt Research Award; held positions at Munich, Birkbeck College London, Manchester, and Vienna.

speakerDetails.name: Tom Carew
speakerDetails.role: Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Dean of Faculty of Arts and Science; Professor of Neural Science, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Trained with Eric Kandel; elected fellow of AAAS and American Academy.

speakerDetails.name: Martin Conway
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Cognitive Psychology, City University London
speakerDetails.bio: Studies human memory for 30+ years; known for pioneering theoretical work on autobiographical memory and neuropsychology research.

speakerDetails.name: Penelope Lewis
speakerDetails.role: Senior Lecturer of Neuroscience, University of Manchester
speakerDetails.bio: Runs Neuroscience and Psychology of Sleep (NaPS) lab; author of The Secret World of Sleep.

title: The Realm of Mystery
description: The roundtable explores Donald Rumsfeld's framework of "known knowns," "known unknowns," and "unknown unknowns." Participants examine how we identify gaps in knowledge, transform unknowns into knowns, and consider whether mystery serves essential roles across scientific, religious, and philosophical domains. The discussion addresses cognitive bias and psychoanalytic perspectives on understanding.

speakerDetails.name: Megan Abbott
speakerDetails.role: Author
speakerDetails.bio: Award-winning novelist with seven published works including Dare Me, The End of Everything, and The Fever (which won International Thriller Writers and Strand Critics awards).

speakerDetails.name: Carol Rovane
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Graduate Studies and former Chair of the Philosophy Department; Lenfest Distinguished Faculty Award recipient. Research focuses on metaphysics, philosophy of mind, action, and ethics.

speakerDetails.name: Michael S. Turner
speakerDetails.role: Bruce V. and Diana M. Rauner Distinguished Service Professor of Physics, University of Chicago
speakerDetails.bio: Theoretical astrophysicist; Director of Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics; former American Physical Society President.

speakerDetails.name: Elliot Wolfson
speakerDetails.role: Marsha and Jay Glazer Chair, Jewish Studies, UC Santa Barbara
speakerDetails.bio: Fellow of American Academy of Jewish Research and Arts & Sciences. Specializes in Jewish mysticism history.

speakerDetails.name: Susan Wolfson
speakerDetails.role: Professor of English, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches British Romanticism literature, Shakespeare, and Milton. Previously at UC Berkeley and Rutgers University.

title: Understanding Genius
description: Schopenhauer's definition of genius contrasts with talent: "Talent hits a target others miss. Genius hits a target no one sees." The roundtable explored whether originality is essential to genius, examined Kant's distinction between aesthetic and scientific genius, explored different genius types, and questioned why child prodigies don't always become adult geniuses.

speakerDetails.name: Steve Hsu
speakerDetails.role: Vice-President for Research and Professor of Theoretical Physics, Michigan State University
speakerDetails.bio: Educated at Caltech and Berkeley; Harvard Junior Fellow; previously held professorships at Yale and University of Oregon; founder and CEO of SafeWeb.

speakerDetails.name: Rex Jung
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Neurosurgery, University of New Mexico
speakerDetails.bio: Trained in clinical psychology and neuropsychology at University of New Mexico; completed internship at Baylor College of Medicine in Neurosurgery and Behavioral Medicine; postdoctoral training in Psychiatry Research.

speakerDetails.name: Darrin McMahon
speakerDetails.role: Mary Brinsmead Wheelock Professor of History, Dartmouth College
speakerDetails.bio: Formerly Ben Weider Professor at Florida State University (2004-2014); educated at UC Berkeley and Yale; PhD 1998.

speakerDetails.name: Joanne Ruthsatz
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Psychology, The Ohio State University, Mansfield
speakerDetails.bio: BA from Bowling Green State University (Phi Beta Kappa); PhD in Experimental Psychology from Case Western Reserve University; studied full range of human cognitive abilities.

speakerDetails.name: Dean Keith Simonton
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of Psychology, University of California, Davis
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in Social Psychology from Harvard (1975); research spans genius, creativity, leadership, talent, and aesthetics; 500+ publications including 13 books.

title: Epigenetics at Work
description: The roundtable explores how Lamarck's theory of inherited characteristics has been revived through the field of epigenetics: the study of alterations in gene expression or phenotype caused by mechanisms other than primary alterations in nucleotide sequence. The discussion examines how epigenetics recasts the nature versus nurture debate through multifactorial inheritance, epistatic interaction, and transcriptomics.

speakerDetails.name: Frances Champagne
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Psychology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Research investigates how genetic and environmental factors interact to shape brain and behavior through epigenetic changes in gene expression, with studies in rodents examining maternal care effects.

speakerDetails.name: Zachary Kaminsky
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Jointly appointed in Bloomberg School of Public Health; earned Ph.D. from University of Toronto studying psychiatric epigenetics.

speakerDetails.name: Fei Li
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Biology, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Molecular Genetics from University of Texas at Austin; conducted postdoctoral research at UT Southwestern and UC Berkeley.

speakerDetails.name: Jessica Tyler
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Department of Epigenetics and Molecular Carcinogenesis, University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center
speakerDetails.bio: Born England 1969; graduated University of Sheffield with Biochemistry degree; Ph.D. from MRC Virology Unit, Glasgow.

title: Human and Nonhuman Minds: Continuities and Discontinuities
description: The event examined animal cognition following Darwin's 1872 work on emotions. The subsequent prodigious scientific study of animal cognition and behavior has answered this question with an emphatic "yes!" The central question evolved from whether animals think to determining the degree and nature of their cognition.

speakerDetails.name: Theodore Dimon
speakerDetails.role: Director, The Dimon Institute; Adjunct Assistant Professor, Columbia Teachers College
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in holistic study of human mental and physical systems using neuroscience and multi-disciplinary approaches.

speakerDetails.name: Stuart Firestein
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neuroscience, Columbia University; Former Chair, Department of Biological Sciences
speakerDetails.bio: Leads research on olfactory neuroscience with 100+ published papers in Nature, Science, and PNAS.

speakerDetails.name: Alexandra Horowitz
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, Barnard College
speakerDetails.bio: Heads the Dog Cognition Lab; research focuses on behavior and mind of owned dogs and animal perception.

speakerDetails.name: Irene Pepperberg
speakerDetails.role: Research Associate, Harvard University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Harvard (1976); visiting positions at Northwestern, University of Arizona, MIT Media Lab, and Brandeis.

speakerDetails.name: Diana Reiss
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, Hunter College; Professor of Biopsychology & Behavioral Neuroscience, CUNY Graduate Center
speakerDetails.bio: Directs dolphin cognitive research programs.

title: Trauma and its Aftereffects, Part I: War and Genocide
description: The roundtable explores what it means to be a survivor of traumatic violence in war and genocide, whether as victim, perpetrator, or descendant. It examines implications for individual and collective conscience regarding state-sanctioned or culturally-consecrated violence.

speakerDetails.name: Adam J. Sacks
speakerDetails.role: Ph.D. Candidate in History, Brown University
speakerDetails.bio: Holds MA from Brown, MS (High Honors) from CUNY City College, BA (Summa Cum Laude, Phi Beta Kappa) from Cornell University.

speakerDetails.name: Ryan Tellalian
speakerDetails.role: Ph.D. Candidate in Clinical Psychology, The New School for Social Research
speakerDetails.bio: MA in Psychology from The New School, M.Div. from St. Vladimir's Orthodox Theological Seminary, Certificate in Armenian Studies from St. Nersess Armenian Seminary; fourth-generation Armenian-American, great-grandson of Genocide survivor.

speakerDetails.name: Gottfried Wagner
speakerDetails.role: Multimedia Director and Publisher
speakerDetails.bio: Musicologist and international lecturer on music and politics; PhD from Vienna; focuses on German culture/politics (19th-20th century) and Jewish history.

speakerDetails.name: Eva Weil
speakerDetails.role: Psychoanalyst, Researcher at the Sorbonne and University Paris I
speakerDetails.bio: Member of Paris Psychoanalytical Society; researcher at Sorbonne, University Paris I, CNRS, and University Paris VII.

speakerDetails.name: Phil Zabriskie
speakerDetails.role: Author and Journalist
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "The Kill Switch" (Kindle Single) about soldiers/Marines and combat trauma; formerly worked overseas as journalist.

title: The Changing Nature of Free Will
description: The roundtable explored how advances in genetics and neuroscience are reshaping our understanding of free will and voluntary choice. Key questions included implications for jurisprudence, the role of quantum mechanical indeterminacy, and whether free will and determinism represent categorically different levels of reality.

speakerDetails.name: Akeel Bilgrami
speakerDetails.role: Sidney Morgenbesser Professor of Philosophy, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Earned B.A. in English Literature from Elphinstone College, Bombay University; Rhodes Scholar at Oxford studying Philosophy, Politics, and Economics; Ph.D. in Philosophy from University of Chicago.

speakerDetails.name: Luis Cabral
speakerDetails.role: Paganelli-Bull Professor of Economics and International Business, Stern School of Business, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Portuguese native; Stanford Ph.D. in Economics (1989); previously taught at London Business School, Berkeley, Yale, and IESE; research focuses on firm competition dynamics.

speakerDetails.name: Brigitte Kahl
speakerDetails.role: Professor of New Testament, Union Theological Seminary in New York; Associate Professor, Religion Department, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Biblical scholar with interdisciplinary and ecological focus; explores scriptural texts in ancient contexts and interpretational trajectories.

speakerDetails.name: Kenneth T. Kishida
speakerDetails.role: Research Scientist, Computational Psychiatry Unit, Virginia Tech Carilion Research Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Investigates neurobiological processes underlying human choice behavior; B.A. in Genetics from UC Davis.

speakerDetails.name: Simon Kochen
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus and Senior Research Scientist, Mathematics Department, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Princeton (1959); professor at Cornell (1960-1967); joined Princeton in 1968 after year at Institute for Advanced Study.

title: The Mind of a Child
description: The roundtable explores how children at different developmental stages understand the world. Key questions addressed include how one-, three-, and five-year-olds conceptualize experiences differently from older children and adults. The discussion emphasizes understanding children's memory, emotion regulation, and conceptualization to improve care for typically developing children and those with developmental disorders like autism.

speakerDetails.name: Patricia Bauer
speakerDetails.role: Asa Griggs Candler Professor of Psychology, Emory University
speakerDetails.bio: Developmental scientist specializing in autobiographical/personal memory development; earned PhD from Miami University; postdoctoral fellow at UC San Diego.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Harris
speakerDetails.role: Victor S. Thomas Professor of Education, Harvard University
speakerDetails.bio: Developmental psychologist studying cognition, emotion, and imagination development; held positions at Lancaster, Free University of Amsterdam, LSE, and Oxford.

speakerDetails.name: Regina Pally
speakerDetails.role: Co-Founder and Assistant Director, Center for Reflective Parenting
speakerDetails.bio: Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst with 35+ years private practice; 25 years studying neuroscience for professionals and public; community-focused child welfare work.

speakerDetails.name: Colin Phillips
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Linguistics & Distinguished Scholar-Teacher, University of Maryland; Director, Maryland Language Science Center
speakerDetails.bio: Combines linguistics, psychology, and cognitive neuroscience studying language mental encoding and children's language acquisition.

speakerDetails.name: Steven Wein
speakerDetails.role: Supervising Child and Adolescent Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute
speakerDetails.bio: NYPSI Supervising Analyst (since 1993), Training Analyst (since 1996), Associate Dean for Child Analysis (2010-2016); Life Fellow, American Psychiatric Association.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Zelinsky
speakerDetails.role: Children's Book Illustrator and Author
speakerDetails.bio: Caldecott Medal winner for Rapunzel; three Caldecott Honors for Hansel and Gretel, Rumpelstiltskin, and Swamp Angel; known for stylistic variety.

title: Curiosity
description: The roundtable explores how curiosity has been seen through the ages as the impulse that drives our knowledge forward alongside its risks as a temptation toward dangerous and forbidden waters. Participants examine fundamental human questions -- "Why does evil exist? What is beauty? How does language inform us?" -- through discussion of Alberto Manguel's book Curiosity (Yale University Press). The event convenes scholars in the sciences and humanities in an exploration with Mr. Manguel of the meaningfulness of lives -- their own and those of others -- lived with, through, and in curiosity.

speakerDetails.name: Alberto Manguel
speakerDetails.role: Writer and translator
speakerDetails.bio: Argentine-Canadian author who directed the Argentine National Library until 2018.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Browde
speakerDetails.role: Psychiatrist and teaching faculty, Department of Narrative Medicine, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in narrative therapy and relational work.

speakerDetails.name: Edgar Choueiri
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Applied Physics, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Engineering Physics Program and Electric Propulsion and Plasma Dynamics Laboratory.

speakerDetails.name: Marie Howe
speakerDetails.role: Poet Laureate of New York State (2012-2014)
speakerDetails.bio: Author of five poetry collections; poet in residence at Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine.

speakerDetails.name: Siri Hustvedt
speakerDetails.role: Author and essayist
speakerDetails.bio: Published seven novels and five essay collections exploring literature, psychology, and cultural topics.

title: Apprehending Consciousness
description: The roundtable explores whether science is nearing an answer to the question of how and why consciousness and self-consciousness come about. It examines roles of physics, psychology, psychoanalysis, and neuroscience in understanding sentience, plus contributions from philosophical and religious traditions.

speakerDetails.name: David Chalmers
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy and Neural Science, New York University; Co-Director, Center for Mind, Brain, & Consciousness
speakerDetails.bio: University Professor at NYU; authored "The Conscious Mind" (1996), "Constructing the World" (2010), "Reality+: Virtual Worlds and the Problems of Philosophy" (2022); co-founded Association for Scientific Study of Consciousness. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/david-chalmers-2/

speakerDetails.name: Karl Friston
speakerDetails.role: Professor at the Institute of Neurology, University College London
speakerDetails.bio: Theoretical neuroscientist specializing in brain imaging; inventor of statistical parametric mapping (SPM), voxel-based morphometry (VBM), and dynamic causal modelling (DCM). Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/karl-friston/

speakerDetails.name: Piet Hut
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Interdisciplinary Studies, Institute for Advanced Study
speakerDetails.bio: Professor of Astrophysics at Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton since 1985; Head of Program for Interdisciplinary Studies; focuses on computational astrophysics and multiscale simulations. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/piet-hut/

speakerDetails.name: Gabrielle Jackson
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Philosophy, Stony Brook University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Philosophy from Harvard (2011); formerly Andrew W Mellon Postdoctoral Fellow at University of Toronto; Visitor at Institute for Advanced Study. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/gabrielle-jackson/

speakerDetails.name: Ken Paller
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology; Director of Cognitive Neuroscience Program, Northwestern University
speakerDetails.bio: Conducts cognitive neuroscience research at Northwestern; directs Training Program in Neuroscience of Human Cognition; research focuses on memory, consciousness, and sleep's role in memory. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/ken-paller/

speakerDetails.name: Nicholas Schiff
speakerDetails.role: Director of Laboratory for Cognitive Neuromodulation at Weill Cornell Medical College; Professor of Neuroscience, Neurology, and Public Health
speakerDetails.bio: Jerold B. Katz Professor; directs integrative translational research on consciousness recovery following brain injuries. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/nicholas-schiff/

title: Particle Fever / The Quest
description: The event centered on Mark Levinson's 2013 documentary "Particle Fever," which tells the remarkable story of the monumental search for the Higgs boson, the elementary force particle predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics. After screening the film, a roundtable discussion explored qualities of mind and character driving scientific discovery and exploration.

speakerDetails.name: Sarah Demers
speakerDetails.role: Horace D. Taft Associate Professor of Physics, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Particle physicist studying fundamental particles and forces of nature; recent work on Higgs Boson characterization with ATLAS Collaboration at CERN's Large Hadron Collider; Harvard BA, UC Berkeley PhD in theoretical physics.

speakerDetails.name: Mark Levinson
speakerDetails.role: Director of Particle Fever
speakerDetails.bio: Earned doctoral degree in theoretical particle physics from UC Berkeley; specialist in ADR post-production work with renowned directors.

speakerDetails.name: Alberto Manguel
speakerDetails.role: Writer and Translator
speakerDetails.bio: Argentinian-Canadian writer and critic; former director of Argentine National Library; recipient of Formentor Prize (2017) and Gutenberg Prize (2018); resides in New York.

speakerDetails.name: Jean Strouse
speakerDetails.role: Historian and Biographer
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "Morgan, American Financier" (1999, 2014) and "Alice James, A Biography" (1980, 2011); Bancroft Prize winner; contributor to major publications.

title: The Sublime Experience
description: The roundtable examined how the sublime evolved from pre-18th century understanding of "beauty and greatness beyond measure" through Edmund Burke's foundational work. Discussion explored awe, the emotion classically associated with the sublime, and its psychological dimensions. The event considered how the sublime manifests differently across visual arts, music, religious experience, and nature, drawing on philosophy, religion, psychology, and neuroscience to distinguish between pleasure and sublime ecstasy.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Fry
speakerDetails.role: William Lampson Professor of English, Emeritus, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: BA Berkeley, Ph.D. Harvard; taught at Yale since 1971. Primary fields include British Romanticism, History of Criticism, Literary Theory, and Literature and Painting. Also a painter and art critic for Art News. Won the Melville Caine Award for The Poet's Calling in the English Ode (1980).

speakerDetails.name: James Judd
speakerDetails.role: Conductor; Music Director of the Israel Symphony and the Little Orchestra Society
speakerDetails.bio: Previously directed New Zealand Symphony, Orchestre National de Lille, Adelaide Symphony, and Florida Philharmonic. Regular guest conductor globally; leads annual Asian Youth Orchestra tours.

speakerDetails.name: Alan Richardson
speakerDetails.role: Professor of English, Boston College
speakerDetails.bio: Degrees from Princeton and Harvard. Romanticist specializing in British Romantic literature and culture, with focus on gender, childhood, education, race, colonialism, and scientific psychology.

speakerDetails.name: Sandra Shapshay
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Philosophy, Indiana University
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. Intellectual History (UPenn, 1992); Ph.D. Philosophy (Columbia, 2001). Interests center on 19th-century German philosophy, particularly Kant and Schopenhauer, plus contemporary aesthetics and ethics.

title: Music to Whose Ears II: Embodied Cognition
description: This follow-up to a 2013 roundtable explores the body's role in musical experience, its perception and cognition, building on previous discussions connecting music and emotion. The event brought together artists and scientists for interdisciplinary dialogue.

speakerDetails.name: Nacho Arimany
speakerDetails.role: Ethnic percussionist and composer
speakerDetails.bio: Master ethnic percussionist, multi-instrumentalist and composer, currently based in New York City with classical training beginning at age six.

speakerDetails.name: Edgar Choueiri
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Applied Physics at Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Director of the Electric Propulsion and Plasma Dynamics Laboratory; associated with multiple departments.

speakerDetails.name: Vijay Iyer
speakerDetails.role: Composer and pianist
speakerDetails.bio: Described as "one of the most interesting and vital young pianists in jazz today" and named 2014 DownBeat Pianist of the Year.

speakerDetails.name: Marina Korsakova-Kreyn
speakerDetails.role: Professional pianist and scholar
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Cognition and Neuroscience; research focuses on emotional responses to music and perception.

speakerDetails.name: Tristan Perich
speakerDetails.role: Composer
speakerDetails.bio: Work inspired by aesthetic simplicity of math, physics and code; released first album as a microchip in 2004.

title: The Search for Immortality
description: The roundtable explores humanity's pursuit of transcending mortality through philosophy, science, and spirituality. Drawing from Plato's Phaedo, it examines how awareness of death shapes our lives and whether scientific advances in perception and spiritual practices offer pathways to "life in the hereafter or in alternative realms."

speakerDetails.name: Martin Hagglund
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Comparative Literature and Humanities, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of Dying for Time: Proust, Woolf, Nabokov (Harvard, 2012) and Radical Atheism (Stanford, 2008); focus on philosophical temporality. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/martin-hagglund/

speakerDetails.name: Chris Impey
speakerDetails.role: University Distinguished Professor of Astronomy, University of Arizona
speakerDetails.bio: Over 220 refereed publications on cosmology, galaxies, quasars; $20M in NASA/NSF grants; eleven teaching awards; taught online courses to 350,000+ students. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/chris-impey/

speakerDetails.name: Adam Kirsch
speakerDetails.role: Senior Editor, The New Republic; Columnist, Tablet Magazine
speakerDetails.bio: Author of poetry collections The Thousand Wells, Invasions, and Rocket and Lightship: Essays on Literature and Ideas. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/adam-kirsch/

speakerDetails.name: Sheldon Solomon
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology; Ross Professor of Interdisciplinary Studies, Skidmore College
speakerDetails.bio: Experimental social psychologist (B.A. Franklin & Marshall, PhD University of Kansas); research on self, consciousness, social behavior. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/sheldon-solomon/

speakerDetails.name: Polly Young-Eisendrath
speakerDetails.role: Psychologist, Jungian Psychoanalyst
speakerDetails.bio: PhD; published 15 books including The Self-Esteem Trap, The Resilient Spirit, Women and Desire, The Present Heart; memoir on love and healing. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/polly-young-eisendrath/

title: French Surrealism: A Revolution of the Mind
description: The event explored French Surrealism beyond its famous visual art. "French Surrealism is probably best known for its paintings -- images of floppy watches or men in bowler hats and topcoats falling from the sky." However, the roundtable emphasized poetry's central role, featuring works by Andre Breton, Robert Desnos, Benjamin Peret, Louis Aragon, and Rene Char. The discussion included poetry readings in translation and historical context spanning the mid-1920s through late 1960s.

speakerDetails.name: Mary Ann Caws
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of English, French, and Comparative Literature, Graduate Center of the City University of New York
speakerDetails.bio: Recipient of Guggenheim, Rockefeller, and Fulbright fellowships; fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences; past President of the Modern Language Association and American Comparative Literature Association. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/mary-ann-caws/

speakerDetails.name: Anne-Marie Levine
speakerDetails.role: Poet and Visual Artist
speakerDetails.bio: NYC-based poet and visual artist; former concert pianist. Author of three poetry collections: Euphorbia, Bus Ride to a Blue Movie, and Oral History; forthcoming artists book Reculer Pour Mieux Sauter. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/anne-marie-levine/

speakerDetails.name: Mark Polizzotti
speakerDetails.role: Author & Translator; Director of Publications Program, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
speakerDetails.bio: Author of Revolution of the Mind: The Life of Andre Breton, Highway 61 Revisited, Sympathy for the Traitor: A Translation Manifesto, Why Surrealism Matters, and Jump Cuts. Published in Apollo, Bookforum, The Brooklyn Rail, The Nation, The New Republic, The New York Times, and The Paris Review. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/mark-polizzotti/

speakerDetails.name: Bill Zavatsky
speakerDetails.role: Poet
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. and M.F.A. from Columbia University. Educator since 1971 at all educational levels; taught at Trinity School in Manhattan and Eugene Lang College of the New School; leads ongoing poetry-writing workshop. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/bill-zavatsky/

title: Complexity and Emergence
description: Psychobiologist Roger Sperry's concept that "mind and consciousness are dynamic emergent properties of the living brain in action" forms the basis for this discussion. The roundtable examines how novel entities arise from self-organizing complex systems and whether scientific predictability remains viable when systems exhibit adaptive properties beyond their component parts. Topics span neuroscience, economics, and political philosophy.

speakerDetails.name: Mark Alford
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Physics, Washington University in Saint Louis
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on particle physics, nuclear physics, and astrophysics, particularly neutron star theory. Ph.D. from Harvard University.

speakerDetails.name: Zosia Krusberg
speakerDetails.role: Visiting Assistant Professor of Physics and Astronomy, Vassar College
speakerDetails.bio: Theoretical particle physicist and cosmologist. Ph.D. from University of Chicago in early universe physics.

speakerDetails.name: Timothy O'Connor
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, Indiana University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of religion. Ph.D. from Cornell University.

speakerDetails.name: Raul Rabadan
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Departments of Systems Biology and Biomedical Informatics, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons

speakerDetails.name: Caleb Scharf
speakerDetails.role: Director of Astrobiology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Research spans cosmology, exoplanetary science, and astrobiology.

title: The Span of Infinity
description: The roundtable explores how no thing conceived in the mind has enjoyed a greater confluence of cosmological, mathematical, philosophical, psychological, and theological inquiry than the notion of the infinite. The event examines the epistemological tension between the concrete and the ideal, investigating humanity's place in the universe and existence's comprehensibility.

speakerDetails.name: Alfred Scharff Goldhaber
speakerDetails.role: Professor in the C.N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics and the Department of Physics and Astronomy, Stony Brook University
speakerDetails.bio: Second-generation physicist; collaborated with parents on research.

speakerDetails.name: Joel David Hamkins
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Mathematics, Philosophy and Computer Science, City University of New York (College of Staten Island and CUNY Graduate Center)
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D., C. Phil. (UC Berkeley); B.S. (Caltech).

speakerDetails.name: Charles Liu
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Astrophysics, City University of New York's College of Staten Island; Hayden Planetarium; American Museum of Natural History
speakerDetails.bio: Focus on colliding galaxies, quasars, universe star formation history.

speakerDetails.name: Eric Steinhart
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, William Paterson University
speakerDetails.bio: B.S. Computer Science (Pennsylvania State University); M.A., Ph.D. Philosophy.

title: Cancer: Body & Mind
description: The roundtable explores cancer through biological and psychological lenses. It addresses historical misconceptions about cancer, referencing Susan Sontag's Illness as Metaphor (1978), which critiqued false psychological-disease connections. The discussion examines modern cellular and molecular biology advances alongside emerging psychoneuroimmunology research revealing mind-body influences on cancer development and immunity.

speakerDetails.name: Andrea Califano
speakerDetails.role: Clyde and Helen Wu Professor of Chemical and Systems Biology, Columbia University (Departments of Biochemistry & Molecular Biophysics and Biomedical Informatics)
speakerDetails.bio: Founding director and chair of the Columbia Initiative for Systems Biology. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/andrea-califano/

speakerDetails.name: Selina Chen-Kiang
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Pathology; Professor of Immunology and Microbial Pathogenesis, Weill-Cornell Medical College
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in Genetics and Development (Columbia); Jane Coffin Child Cancer Fellow; postdoctoral training at Rockefeller University. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/selina-chen-kiang/

speakerDetails.name: Susan Lutgendorf
speakerDetails.role: Professor in Departments of Psychology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, and Urology, University of Iowa; Holden Comprehensive Cancer Center
speakerDetails.bio: Her current work, funded by the National Cancer Institute, examines how factors such as stress, depression, and social support are linked to biological processes involved in angiogenesis. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/susan-lutgendorf/

speakerDetails.name: Hans-Guido Wendel
speakerDetails.role: Principal Investigator, Cancer Genetics Laboratory, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center
speakerDetails.bio: Trained in medicine (Aachen and Edinburgh); identifies new cancer therapies based on genetic disease origins. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/hans-guido-wendel/

title: Knowledge and Limitations
description: The roundtable explores fundamental questions about human knowledge: "What do we know about the universe and how do we know it?" Drawing from John Locke's inquiry into knowledge's extent and boundaries, the discussion examines whether our grasp of natural laws faces cognitive or linguistic constraints, or if inherent physical and mathematical limitations exist. The event considers whether metaphysics -- philosophy addressing first principles and imperceptible realms -- can integrate with empirical epistemology.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph Kohn
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus of Mathematics, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Born Prague, May 18, 1932; emigrated to Ecuador (1939), then US (1945). BS MIT 1953; PhD Princeton 1956. Taught Brandeis (1958-1968), Princeton (1968+). Research focuses on theory of several complex variables.

speakerDetails.name: Tim Maudlin
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: BA Physics and Philosophy (Yale); PhD History and Philosophy of Science (University of Pittsburgh). Specializes in interpreting physical theory and understanding mathematical structures in physics.

speakerDetails.name: Priyamvada Natarajan
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Astronomy and Physics, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Research addresses dark matter, dark energy, and black holes. Notable contributions include mapping dark matter distribution and tracing black hole growth history using gravitational lensing.

speakerDetails.name: Dorothea von Mucke
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Germanic Languages and Literatures, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Comparative Literature (Stanford); teaching at Columbia since 1988. Visiting professorships in Berlin and Giessen.

title: Responses: Poetry with Jean Valentine and Patrick Rosal
description: The "Responses" series involves poets reading aloud each other's work and offering commentary. This inaugural event featured two accomplished poets as participants.

speakerDetails.name: Patrick Rosal
speakerDetails.role: Poet
speakerDetails.bio: Author of three full-length poetry collections, including Boneshepherds, which received recognition from the National Book Critics Circle and Academy of American Poets. He has won the Association of Asian American Studies Book Award, Global Filipino Literary Award, and Asian American Writers Workshop Members' Choice Award. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/patrick-rosal/

speakerDetails.name: Jean Valentine
speakerDetails.role: Poet
speakerDetails.bio: Contributing to literature for approximately fifty years. Her debut, Dream Barker and Other Poems, won the Yale Younger Poets Prize in 1965. Door in the Mountain: New and Collected Poems, 1965-2003 won the National Book Award in 2004. Recent work includes Break the Glass. Profile: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/jean-valentine-3/

title: Women and the Work World
description: "The last 50 years has seen increasing parity of opportunity for, and achievement by, women in the work world as reflected in their increasing numbers in leadership roles in medicine and other sciences, academe, business, and politics." The roundtable examined obstacles to women's employment and career advancement, considering cultural, psychological, and biological causes and consequences.

speakerDetails.name: Graciela Chichilnisky
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Economics, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Columbia Consortium for Risk Management; world-renowned economist credited with creating formal theory of Sustainable Development.

speakerDetails.name: Marit Delozier
speakerDetails.role: Lawyer and Assistant District Attorney, New York City
speakerDetails.bio: Prosecutor for Manhattan DA's Office; previously clerked for DC Court of Appeals and served as legal counsel to Senate Judiciary Committee.

speakerDetails.name: Nancy DiTomaso
speakerDetails.role: Vice Dean for Faculty and Research, Rutgers University Business School
speakerDetails.bio: Professor of Management and Global Business; research focuses on diversity management, knowledge-based organizations.

speakerDetails.name: Ernesto Reuben
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Management, Columbia Business School
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in behavioral and public economics; studies social norms and psychological traits.

speakerDetails.name: Patricia Taylor
speakerDetails.role: Chair, Women's International Advisory Council, International House
speakerDetails.bio: Former Head of National Hepatitis Reference Laboratory in Ottawa.

title: Women and Science
