description: The roundtable opens with historical context, referencing a 4,700-year-old Egyptian hieroglyph identifying Merit-Ptah as "the Chief Physician." The event examines gender gaps in STEM fields, exploring how disparities widen through undergraduate, graduate, postdoctoral, and academic career stages. Key questions addressed include whether scientific abilities differ by gender, the relative influences of nature versus nurture, and the prevalence of sexism in scientific professions. The discussion encompasses challenges faced by successful women scientists and strategies for advancing equal opportunity.

speakerDetails.name: Cristina Alberini
speakerDetails.role: Professor in the Center for Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Twenty-year researcher studying biological mechanisms of long-term memory, focusing on consolidation and reconsolidation, the processes by which newly learned information become long-lasting memories.

speakerDetails.name: Priyamvada Natarajan
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Astronomy and Physics, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on dark matter, dark energy, and black holes. Known for gravitational lensing contributions addressing two of the most challenging problems in cosmology.

speakerDetails.name: Liz Phelps
speakerDetails.role: Julius Silver Professor of Psychology and Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from Princeton (1989), former Yale faculty (until 1999). Laboratory conducts groundbreaking research on how the human brain processes emotion.

speakerDetails.name: Tal Rabin
speakerDetails.role: Research Staff Member and Manager of Cryptographic Research Group, IBM T.J. Watson Research Center
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on secure multiparty computation, threshold cryptography and proactive security.

speakerDetails.name: Anna Ziegler
speakerDetails.role: Playwright
speakerDetails.bio: Works produced at major theaters including Seattle Repertory Theatre, Cincinnati Playhouse, and various regional venues.

title: Synchronicity: On the Spectrum of Mind and Matter
description: The roundtable explores synchronicity -- meaningful coincidence of two or more causally unrelated events sharing similar meaning -- developed by physicist Wolfgang Pauli and psychiatrist C.G. Jung. The discussion examines how physics and psychology explore mind on a continuum with matter, addressing synchronistic phenomena that operate acausally and manifest at intersections of objective and subjective experience.

speakerDetails.name: Harald Atmanspacher
speakerDetails.role: Physicist, The Collegium Helveticum (ETH Zurich, Switzerland)
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in physics from Munich University (1986). Senior scientist at Collegium Helveticum, University of Zurich and ETH Zurich since 2007. Previously worked at Max-Planck-Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics until 1998; headed theory group.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph Cambray
speakerDetails.role: Jungian Analyst; Past President, International Association of Analytical Psychology
speakerDetails.bio: Faculty member at Harvard Medical School's Center for Psychoanalytic Studies and Massachusetts General Hospital's Psychiatry Department. Adjunct faculty at Pacifica Graduate Institute. Former US Editor of the Journal of Analytical Psychology.

speakerDetails.name: Edgar Choueiri
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Applied Physics, Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering; Associated Faculty, Department of Astrophysical Sciences and Program in Plasma Physics, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Princeton's Program in Engineering Physics and Electric Propulsion and Plasma Dynamics Laboratory (EPPDyL). Tenured Full Professor in Applied Physics Group.

speakerDetails.name: Farzad Mahootian
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Associate Professor of Global Liberal Studies, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Interdisciplinary background (PhD Philosophy, Fordham; MS Chemistry, Georgetown). Research focuses on interactions between philosophy, science and society within technoscience's mythological imagination, guided by process philosophy, biomimicry, and artificial intelligence.

speakerDetails.name: Beverley Zabriskie
speakerDetails.role: Jungian Analyst; Founding faculty member and past President, New York's Jungian Psychoanalytic Association (JPA)
speakerDetails.bio: Associate editor, Journal of Analytical Psychology (London). Board Member of The Philemon Foundation (producing Jung's unpublished works). Authored approximately 60 publications including "Time and Tao in Synchronicity" in The Pauli-Jung Conjecture.

title: Identity and Fanaticism
description: The roundtable explored how biological, developmental, and social influences transform individuals into group members, and when ethnic, religious, or national identity crosses from affiliation into fanaticism. It featured quotes from Einstein and Freud's "Why War?" correspondence examining power dynamics and emotional bonds within groups.

speakerDetails.name: Chip Gagnon
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Politics at Ithaca College
speakerDetails.bio: Long-time Visiting Scholar at Cornell University's Judith Reppy Institute for Peace and Conflict Studies; Ph.D. in Political Science from Columbia University with focus on International Relations and certificates in Soviet/Russian and East European Studies.

speakerDetails.name: Elise Giuliano
speakerDetails.role: Lecturer in Political Science at Columbia University; Academic advisor at Columbia's Harriman Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Political scientist teaching secession, nationalism, and Russian politics; research focuses on politics-identity intersection.

speakerDetails.name: Liah Greenfeld
speakerDetails.role: University Professor and Professor of Sociology, Political Science, and Anthropology at Boston University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of works on nationalism and economic growth; published by Harvard University Press (1992, 2001, 2013).

speakerDetails.name: Leora Kahn
speakerDetails.role: Founder and President of PROOF: Media for Social Justice
speakerDetails.bio: Works with Amnesty International and UN; authored "Darfur: 20 years of War and Genocide" (2007).

speakerDetails.name: Nathan M. Szajnberg
speakerDetails.role: Wallerstein Research Fellow in Psychoanalysis, San Francisco Center for Psychoanalysis
speakerDetails.bio: Faculty member at New York Psychoanalytic Society; formerly Freud Professor at Hebrew University; author/editor of four books.

title: Biology of Mind
description: The roundtable explored fundamental questions about consciousness and cognition: "What is mind? Is it a property attributable to biological functionality alone, and, in particular, arising from the morphology of the mammalian brain and/or the influence of that animal's body? How far down the evolutionary scale can we apply terms like cognition, consciousness, and intelligence? Are we capable of engineering artificial minds?"

speakerDetails.name: John Krakauer
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neurology and Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: John C. Malone Professor at the Malone Center for Engineering in Healthcare; also Professor of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation; Director of the Brain, Learning, Animation, and Movement Lab (BLAM Lab); Co-founder of the KATA project.

speakerDetails.name: Gary Marcus
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, New York University; Director, NYU Center for Language and Music
speakerDetails.bio: Described by New York Times as "one of the country's best known cognitive psychologists"; published on language, evolution, computation, and cognitive development; authored four books including Kluge, The Algebraic Mind, and Guitar Zero.

speakerDetails.name: Kenneth Miller
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neuroscience, Columbia University; Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience; co-Director of the Center for Theoretical Neuroscience
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. Reed College; M.S. and Ph.D. Stanford University; postdoctoral work at UCSF and Caltech.

speakerDetails.name: David Rosenthal
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, CUNY Graduate Center; Coordinator of the Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science
speakerDetails.bio: Specialization: Consciousness, representational character of mental states.

speakerDetails.name: Matthew Stone
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Department of Computer Science, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from University of Pennsylvania (1998). Visiting positions at University of Edinburgh.

title: From Children's Sights to Our Insights: Ethiopian Children's Drawings, Stories and Inner Lives
description: A study by Nathan Szajnberg featured Ethiopian/Israeli six-year-old children's drawings depicting their lives, fantasies, fears, hopes, and wishes. Roundtable participants applied art historical, linguistic, and psychoanalytic perspectives to examine representation, developmental transitions from visual to narrative expression, and universal versus culture-specific dimensions of human experience.

speakerDetails.name: Theodore Shapiro
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus, Weill-Cornell Medical College
speakerDetails.bio: Psychoanalyst and adult/child/adolescent psychiatrist; co-principal investigator on psychodynamic psychotherapy research for anxious youth; over 200 scholarly publications and 7 authored books.

speakerDetails.name: Ellen Handler Spitz
speakerDetails.role: Honors College Professor of Visual Arts, University of Maryland (UMBC)
speakerDetails.bio: Writes and teaches on visual, literary, and performing arts alongside psychology; research candidate at Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training; 2008 Erikson Scholar at Austen Riggs.

speakerDetails.name: Nathan M. Szajnberg
speakerDetails.role: Wallerstein Research Fellow in Psychoanalysis, San Francisco Center for Psychoanalysis
speakerDetails.bio: Faculty member at New York Psychoanalytic Society; former Freud Professor of Psychoanalysis at Hebrew University; author/editor of four books and one novella on psychoanalysis and education.

title: Secrecy and Transparency
description: The internet enables unprecedented sharing and manipulation of individual and social information, with implications for privacy, healthcare, citizenship, national security, and concepts of personhood and institutional power. This roundtable explores contemporary privacy notions, data exchange relationships between individuals and institutions, the role of secrets in self and emotion, and tensions between secrecy and transparency in protecting individual freedoms.

speakerDetails.name: Alex Abdo
speakerDetails.role: Staff Attorney, American Civil Liberties Union National Security Project
speakerDetails.bio: Counsel in ACLU's challenge to NSA phone-records program; involved in litigation concerning Patriot Act, FISA, International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and Guantanamo detainee treatment

speakerDetails.name: Jack Z. Bratich
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor and Chair, Department of Journalism and Media Studies, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Applies autonomist social theory to popular culture and social movement media; zine librarian at ABC No Rio; co-taught courses at Bluestockings Bookstore, NYC

speakerDetails.name: Elizabeth Haase
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Clinical Professor, Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst in private practice; member of Helix Center Executive Committee; editor, writer, teacher for psychiatric associations

speakerDetails.name: Ted Jacobs
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Professor of Psychiatry Emeritus, Albert Einstein College of Medicine; Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst
speakerDetails.bio: Board-certified psychiatrist; training analyst at multiple psychoanalytic institutes

speakerDetails.name: Michael Lewis
speakerDetails.role: University Distinguished Professor of Pediatrics and Psychiatry, Director of Institute for Study of Child Development, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: Also Professor of Psychology, Education, Biomedical Engineering, and Social Work at Rutgers; serves on Executive Committee of Center for Cognitive Sciences

title: The Amygdaloids Warburg Symposium Concert
description: A New York-based band composed of scientists performing songs about "love and life peppered with insights drawn from research about mind and brain and mental disorders." The performance included multiple song suites addressing topics including the mind-body problem, unconscious brain function, memory, and fear/anxiety, each preceded by brief neuroscience discussions.

title: Altruism and Empathy
description: The roundtable explores whether selflessness represents a necessary illusion and examines the tension between evolutionary adaptation and pure altruism. It investigates how humans develop "theory of mind" around age three, enabling empathy and compassion. Key questions include whether altruistic acts can remain untainted by self-interest or reveal "the better angels of our nature."

speakerDetails.name: Stephanie Brown
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Preventive Medicine, SUNY Stony Brook; Adjunct Assistant Professor, Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan
speakerDetails.bio: Focuses on neuro-affective mechanisms underlying altruistic and prosocial behavior, examining other-focused motivational states in stress contexts

speakerDetails.name: Lisa Cataldo
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Pastoral Care and Counseling, Fordham University Graduate School of Religion and Religious Education
speakerDetails.bio: M.Div., Ph.D.; licensed psychoanalyst; directs Clinical Program; teaches Clinical Practice, Professional Ethics, Psychology and Religion, and Trauma

speakerDetails.name: Alan Leslie
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Science, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Fellow, Association for Psychological Science and American Academy of Arts and Sciences; directs Cognitive Development Laboratory; investigates developmental neurocognitive mechanisms

speakerDetails.name: Wynn Schwartz
speakerDetails.role: Clinical psychologist and research psychoanalyst, Massachusetts School of Professional Psychology; faculty at Harvard Medical School and Harvard Extension School
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D.; previously professor at Wellesley College; coeditor of Advances in Descriptive Psychology

title: Second Annual Heavy MeNtal Variety Show
description: "A night of mind, brain, and magic. The Amygdaloids will play several suites of our original songs on mind/brain topics: the mind-body problem, memory, emotion, unconscious processes, and mental disorders." Each musical suite was preceded by a 3-minute lecture on scientific/philosophical foundations by neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux. Magician Mark Mitton performed during intermission.

title: Synthetic and Systems Biology: Reinventing the Code of Life
description: The roundtable explores how synthetic and systems biology enable DNA reengineering at unprecedented pace. These interdisciplinary fields combine biology, engineering, computer science, and neuroscience to develop novel therapeutics, energy sources, disease treatments, and life extension. Discussion centers on whether these fields represent the arrival of "Promethean Man" -- humanity achieving transformative biological capabilities -- while examining both aspirations and risks.

speakerDetails.name: Andrea Califano
speakerDetails.role: Clyde and Helen Wu Professor of Chemical and Systems Biology, Columbia University (Departments of Biochemistry & Molecular Biophysics; Biomedical Informatics)
speakerDetails.bio: Founding director and chair, Columbia Initiative for Systems Biology; Associate Director for Bioinformatics, Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center

speakerDetails.name: Mark Fishman, M.D.
speakerDetails.role: President, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research
speakerDetails.bio: Previously Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School; Chief of Cardiology, Massachusetts General Hospital

speakerDetails.name: Michael Hecht
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Chemistry, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Appointments in Department of Molecular Biology; Institute for Integrative Genomics; research focus on protein design, synthetic biology, Alzheimer's disease molecular mechanisms

speakerDetails.name: Christopher Mason
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor in Physiology and Biophysics, Weill Cornell Medical College; Institute for Computational Biomedicine
speakerDetails.bio: Tri-Institutional Program on Computational Biology and Medicine (Cornell, Memorial Sloan-Kettering, Rockefeller University); Weill Cornell Cancer Center

speakerDetails.name: Saeed Tavazoie
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Biochemistry, Molecular Biophysics, and Systems Biology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Previously professor at Princeton University's Department of Molecular Biology and Institute for Integrative Genomics; research in regulatory genome decoding and gene network interactions

speakerDetails.name: Michael Waldholz
speakerDetails.role: Medical Science Writer and Media Consultant
speakerDetails.bio: Managing editor at Bloomberg News/Businessweek (6 years); Wall Street Journal writer, editor, and bureau chief (25 years); covered healthcare, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and health policy

title: Ignorance and Curiosity
description: Physics Nobel laureate David Gross asserts that "the most important product of science is ignorance." The event explores how science pursues better questions alongside knowledge, with curiosity serving as its driving force. Topics include: understanding what we don't know, the nature of curiosity as a mental process, and applications to education, research, and policy.

speakerDetails.name: Heather Berlin
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Psychiatry and Neuroscience, Mount Sinai School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Cognitive neuroscientist exploring brain-mind interactions related to impulsive and compulsive psychiatric disorders Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/heather-berlin/

speakerDetails.name: Susan Engel
speakerDetails.role: Senior Lecturer in Psychology; Director of Program in Teaching, Williams College
speakerDetails.bio: Researches children's narratives, play development, and curiosity with publications in cognitive development journals Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/susan-engel/

speakerDetails.name: Stuart Firestein
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neuroscience; Former Chair, Department of Biological Sciences, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Leads prominent olfactory neuroscience laboratory; published 100+ scientific papers in Nature, Science, PNAS Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/stuart-firestein/

speakerDetails.name: Paul Harris
speakerDetails.role: Victor S. Thomas Professor of Education, Harvard
speakerDetails.bio: Developmental psychologist studying cognition, emotion, and imagination development Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/paul-harris-2/

speakerDetails.name: Alan Hirshfeld
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Physics, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Associate, Harvard College Observatory
speakerDetails.bio: Author of books on cosmic measurement and scientific history Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/alan-hirshfeld/

title: Music to Whose Ears? Music, Emotion, and Mind
description: The roundtable explores Leonard Meyer's 1956 treatise examining philosophical positions on musical meaning. Key questions addressed include how musical meaning might be defined -- whether it exists within the work itself, refers to extra-musical concepts and emotions, stems from formal analysis, or arises from emotional listener response. The discussion examines what creates aesthetic effects in music and whether emotional responses are universal or individually particular.

speakerDetails.name: Greg Calbi
speakerDetails.role: Senior Mastering Engineer, Sterling Sound, New York
speakerDetails.bio: Partner and mastering engineer combining technical expertise with emotional understanding of music, manipulating frequency and dynamics over forty years.

speakerDetails.name: Jesse Harris
speakerDetails.role: Songwriter/Singer/Producer
speakerDetails.bio: Grammy Award-winning artist who wrote "Don't Know Why" for Norah Jones and produces musicians globally.

speakerDetails.name: Marina Korsakova-Kreyn
speakerDetails.role: Pianist and Scholar in Music Perception and Cognition
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Cognition and Neuroscience from University of Texas at Dallas; research focuses on emotional responses to music perception.

speakerDetails.name: Gilbert Rose
speakerDetails.role: Member, Muriel Gardiner Program in Psychoanalysis and the Humanities, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Former Yale Medical School faculty member; award-winning psychoanalyst specializing in psychoanalysis and humanities.

speakerDetails.name: Alina Rubinstein
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Instructor, Department of Psychiatry, NYU School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Psychoanalyst in private practice; faculty member at Institute for Psychoanalytic Education affiliated with NYU Medical Center.

title: Elizabeth Bishop: A Conversation about Her Poetry
description: The event features "one of the great masters of American poetry of the 20th Century" (Elizabeth Bishop, 1911-1979). The roundtable highlights her "skill at recounting the results of her capacity for observation," with participants discussing her work and reading aloud from her poems. Randall Jarrell's observation about Bishop's first book: "All her poems have written underneath, 'I have seen it.'"

speakerDetails.name: Bonnie Costello
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Boston University
speakerDetails.bio: Scholar concentrating on modern and contemporary poetry. Author of Marianne Moore: Imaginary Possessions (1981) and Elizabeth Bishop: Questions of Mastery (1991); general editor of The Selected Letters of Marianne Moore (1997) Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/bonnie-costello/

speakerDetails.name: Alice Quinn
speakerDetails.role: Executive Director, Poetry Society of America
speakerDetails.bio: Adjunct professor at Columbia University's Graduate School of the Arts; former Poetry Editor of The New Yorker (two decades); former editor at Alfred A. Knopf Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/alice-quinn/

speakerDetails.name: Lloyd Schwartz
speakerDetails.role: Frederick S. Troy Professor of English, University of Massachusetts Boston
speakerDetails.bio: Poet and literary critic; classical music editor for The Boston Phoenix; NPR's Fresh Air commentator; 1994 Pulitzer Prize winner for Criticism Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/lloyd-schwartz/

speakerDetails.name: Jean Valentine
speakerDetails.role: Poet
speakerDetails.bio: Contributing poet for half a century; Dream Barker and Other Poems won Yale Younger Poets Prize (1965); Door in the Mountain: New and Collected Poems, 1965-2003 won National Book Award (2004); recent work: Break the Glass Profile URL: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/jean-valentine-3/

title: The Topology of Fear
description: The roundtable explores how emotions influence decision-making, particularly regarding fear and risk assessment. Key topics include responses to catastrophic threats like climate change and species extinction, plus how topology -- a mathematical field -- can redefine rationality to encompass ambiguity and contradictions present in logical systems.

speakerDetails.name: Graciela Chichilnisky
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Economics, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: World-renowned economist; Director of Columbia Consortium for Risk Management; creator of formal theory of Sustainable Development; served as Lead US Author Profile URL: helixcenter.org/participants/graciela-chichilnisky/

speakerDetails.name: Paul Glimcher
speakerDetails.role: Director of Center for Neuroeconomics, New York University; Julius Silver Professor of Neural Science, Economics, and Psychology
speakerDetails.bio: NYU's Center for Neural Science; National Eye Institute Investigator Profile URL: helixcenter.org/participants/paul-glimcher/

speakerDetails.name: Linda Keen
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Mathematics, Graduate Center and Lehman College, CUNY
speakerDetails.bio: Executive Officer of Doctoral Program in Mathematics; expertise in complex analysis, complex dynamics, hyperbolic manifolds, Teichmuller theory Profile URL: helixcenter.org/participants/linda-keen/

speakerDetails.name: Joseph LeDoux
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: National Academy of Sciences member; American Academy of Arts and Sciences member; multiple awards recipient; focus on emotion, memory, consciousness and brain interactions Profile URL: helixcenter.org/participants/joseph-ledoux/

speakerDetails.name: David Lichtenstein
speakerDetails.role: Co-Founder, Apres-Coup Psychoanalytic Association, New York
speakerDetails.bio: Faculty member, supervisor; Editor of DIVISION/Review: A Quarterly Psychoanalytic Forum; Adjunct Professor at CUNY and Adelphi University Profile URL: helixcenter.org/participants/david-lichtenstein/

title: Love, the Interrogative
description: The roundtable explores the nature of love through multiple disciplines. Milan Kundera's concept that "love is a continual interrogation" frames the discussion, examining whether love constitutes a single emotion, a complex of feelings, or a neurochemical phenomenon. The event considers distinctions between parental, romantic, and other love types through historical, neuroscientific, psychoanalytic, poetic, and other analytical lenses.

speakerDetails.name: Andrea Bayer
speakerDetails.role: Department of European Paintings, The Metropolitan Museum of Art
speakerDetails.bio: Works since 1989 in museum departments; involved in Renaissance exhibitions

speakerDetails.name: Lucy L. Brown
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Professor in Neurology, Einstein College of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Experimental/Physiological Psychology (NYU, 1973); expertise in dopamine neurons and brain mapping

speakerDetails.name: Michael Klein
speakerDetails.role: Poet, Essayist
speakerDetails.bio: Lambda Literary Award finalist; award-winning poetry collections and essays

speakerDetails.name: Fred Sander
speakerDetails.role: Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Weill Cornell Department of Psychiatry
speakerDetails.bio: Psychoanalysis and family therapy practitioner since 1963; faculty member at New York Psychoanalytic Institute

speakerDetails.name: Dan Slater
speakerDetails.role: Journalist, Author
speakerDetails.bio: Former Wall Street Journal legal affairs reporter; author of "Love in the Time of Algorithms"

title: Urdu Poetry: Ghalib and the Ghazal
description: The event focuses on "Plaintiffs in Paper Robes: The First Ghazal of Mirza Asadullah Khan Ghalib." Speakers examine the poetry of Ghalib and the ghazal form by analyzing the opening verse of his first ghazal. "An Urdu ghazal consists of a series of miniature poems, each two lines long," allowing exploration of the entire genre within a concise framework.

speakerDetails.name: Frances Pritchett
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Modern Indic Languages, Department of Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African Studies, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in classical Urdu ghazal, particularly Ghalib and Mir works, and traditional narrative genres in Urdu and Hindi. Her translations and commentary on Ghalib's ghazals are available for research.

speakerDetails.name: Mustafa Menai
speakerDetails.role: Lecturer of Urdu, South Asia Studies Department, University of Pennsylvania
speakerDetails.bio: Interests include pedagogy of teaching language through literature and experimenting with poetic structures such as ghazal, nazm, and haiku.

title: Animal Language
description: The roundtable explores "multiple adaptive strategies for the efficient transmission of information" across animal species. The event examines "the phonics and sonics of animal communication," focusing on how "sonic waves -- undersea and above ground" are received through diverse structures like skin, bone, and stomach. Participants investigate connections between animal vocalization systems and human interpretive technologies, "from computer speech to the expressiveness of Beethoven."

speakerDetails.name: Christopher W. Clark
speakerDetails.role: Imogene P. Johnson Director, Bioacoustics Research Program, Cornell University Lab of Ornithology

speakerDetails.name: Ray Dougherty
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Linguistics, New York University

speakerDetails.name: James L. Fuller
speakerDetails.role: Research Fellow, Columbia University

speakerDetails.name: James Higham
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Biological Anthropology, New York University

speakerDetails.name: Diana Reiss
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychology, Hunter College; Professor of Biopsychology & Behavioral Neuroscience, The Graduate Center, CUNY

title: Male-Male Competition: Globalization, War, and Violence
description: The roundtable examines Darwin's focus on male-male competition in The Descent of Man, where he devoted twelve chapters to what he termed "the law of battle." The discussion explores how this phenomenon manifests across species and specifically in humans, noting that modern research addresses it obliquely through "sperm competition." While not universally followed, the pattern appears significant in human history.

speakerDetails.name: R. Brian Ferguson
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Anthropology, Rutgers University-Newark
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Columbia University (1988) focusing on economic and social change in Puerto Rican villages; primary research areas include war and political violence in tribal societies

speakerDetails.name: John Horgan
speakerDetails.role: Science Journalist; Director, Center for Science Writings, Stevens Institute of Technology
speakerDetails.bio: Former senior writer at Scientific American (1986-1997); published in The New York Times, Time, Newsweek, and numerous other publications

speakerDetails.name: E. James Lieberman
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Professor of Psychiatry (Emeritus), George Washington University School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: 40-year psychotherapy practice in Washington D.C.; former Chief, Center for Child and Family Mental Health at NIMH; published extensively on Otto Rank

speakerDetails.name: Maxine Sheets-Johnstone
speakerDetails.role: Courtesy Professor of Philosophy, University of Oregon
speakerDetails.bio: Philosopher with background as dancer/choreographer; published in humanities, art, and science journals

title: Life and Movement
description: The roundtable explored how "evolution, coordination dynamics, sports, social interactions, and aesthetics help us understand movement and life." Key topics included distinguishing "movement and objects as distinctively different things to study," coordination dynamics, kinesthesia, evolution of social coordination, and "how, in the living company of others, we are both challenged and supported."

speakerDetails.name: Jesus Ilundain-Agurruza
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Philosophy, Linfield College
speakerDetails.bio: Received 2011-2012 Samuel H. Graf Faculty Achievement Award; 2008-2009 Allen & Pat Kelley Faculty Scholar; conference chair for International Association for the Philosophy of Sport; co-editor of "Cycling -- Philosophy for Everyone"

speakerDetails.name: Albert A. Johnstone
speakerDetails.role: Courtesy Professor of Philosophy, University of Oregon
speakerDetails.bio: Philosopher with international presentations; author of "Epistemology: Taking Solipsism Seriously" and scholarly papers including "The Deep Bodily Roots of Emotion" (2012) and "The Basic Self and Its Doubles" (2011)

speakerDetails.name: J. A. Scott Kelso
speakerDetails.role: Glenwood and Martha Creech Chair in Science, Florida Atlantic University
speakerDetails.bio: Educated at universities in Belfast, Calgary, and Wisconsin; senior research scientist at Yale's Haskins Laboratories for 7 years before joining Florida Atlantic University in 1985

speakerDetails.name: Maxine Sheets-Johnstone
speakerDetails.role: Courtesy Professor of Philosophy, University of Oregon
speakerDetails.bio: Philosopher with background as dancer/choreographer and dance professor; published extensively in humanities, art, and science journals

title: Collaborations: Jazz and Poetry
description: The roundtable explores jazz poetry as a literary form. Key questions include how written words can express "this blues-based, improvisatory, aural form" and whether jazz-related writing merely describes the genre or accomplishes something deeper. The discussion examines how poems respond to jazz's musical and cultural dimensions, and how written art conveys oral traditions. The event featured Porter performing piano while Singer read poetry to demonstrate their collaborative process.

speakerDetails.name: Lewis Porter
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Music, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Jazz educator and author known for celebrated writings on John Coltrane. Active jazz pianist, keyboardist, and composer with international concert experience. Website: Lewisporter.com

speakerDetails.name: Sean Singer
speakerDetails.role: Poet
speakerDetails.bio: First book Discography won Yale Series of Younger Poets Prize (selected by W.S. Merwin) and Norma Farber First Book Award from Poetry Society of America. Published two chapbooks with Beard of Bees Press.

title: Why Do Economists Disagree?
description: "A pre-election roundtable of a politically diverse group of noted economic theorists exploring their philosophical convergences and divergences."

speakerDetails.name: Graciela Chichilnisky

speakerDetails.bio: Writes "Economic View" column for The New York Times (since 2005); B.S. in mathematics from Georgia Tech

speakerDetails.name: Jeffrey Miron

speakerDetails.bio: Editor of Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics; Academic Vice President of relevant organization; Ph.D. from Rutgers University

title: What Can Mathematics Teach Us About Mind/Brain?
description: "Philosophy meets mathematics meets neuroscience in this roundtable investigating how cutting-edge mathematical models are elucidating the computational rules encoding brain functions and the implications for a deeper understanding of mind."

speakerDetails.name: Ned Block
speakerDetails.role: Silver Professor of Philosophy, Psychology and Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Harvard; came to NYU in 1996 from MIT where he was Chair of the Philosophy Program. Works in philosophy of mind and foundations of neuroscience and cognitive science.

speakerDetails.name: G. Bard Ermentrout
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished University Professor of Computational Biology and Professor of Mathematics, University of Pittsburgh
speakerDetails.bio: BA and MA (mathematics) at Johns Hopkins University; PhD in biophysics & theoretical biology from University of Chicago in 1979. Author of over 200 papers.

speakerDetails.name: Kenneth Miller
speakerDetails.role: Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience; Co-Director, Center for Theoretical Neuroscience, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. from Reed College, M.S. and Ph.D. (with distinction) from Stanford University.

speakerDetails.name: George Reeke, Jr.
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor & Head, Laboratory of Biological Modeling, The Rockefeller University
speakerDetails.bio: B.S. from Caltech, M.A. and Ph.D. from Harvard University.

speakerDetails.name: Xiao-Jing Wang
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neurobiology; Director, Swartz Program in Theoretical Neuroscience, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Adjunct Professor of Physics, Applied Mathematics and Psychology at Yale; held visiting positions at MIT, Ecole Normale Superieure, and Tsinghua University.

title: Where Does It End?
description: The roundtable explores complementary questions about endings, asking "why are we curious about endings, whether that of the cosmos or our own?" It examines organizational properties necessary to define endings and how conceptualizations of consciousness, life, civilization, and universal conclusions inform one another.

speakerDetails.name: James Berger
speakerDetails.role: Senior Lecturer in American Studies and English, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. from Columbia University; M.A. from Teachers College, Columbia; Ph.D. from University of Virginia. Research interests include 20th-21st century American literature, literary theory, disability studies, neuroscience and literature, and apocalyptic literature/film.

speakerDetails.name: William Koblener
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Bar-Ilan University
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. from Columbia College; M.A. from University College, Oxford; Ph.D. from Columbia University. Published in scholarly journals on literature, history, theology, psychoanalysis, cultural criticism, and Jewish studies.

speakerDetails.name: Michael Rampino
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Biology, Earth & Environmental Studies, New York University; Research Consultant at NASA Goddard Institute
speakerDetails.bio: B.A. from Hunter College; Ph.D. in Geological Sciences from Columbia University. Researches mass extinctions and cyclical comet showers.

speakerDetails.name: Paul J. Steinhardt
speakerDetails.role: Albert Einstein Professor in Science and Director, Princeton Center for Theoretical Science, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: B.S. in Physics from Caltech; M.A. and Ph.D. in physics. Faculty member in Physics and Astrophysical Sciences departments.

title: Where Does It Begin?
description: The roundtable explores fundamental questions: "Why are we curious about beginnings, whether that of the cosmos or our own?" Participants examine what can be learned from shared curiosity about origins, the organizational properties defining a beginning, and whether similar processes govern both individual consciousness and universal phenomena.

speakerDetails.name: Chris Impey
speakerDetails.role: University Distinguished Professor, Astronomy, University of Arizona
speakerDetails.bio: Over 220 refereed publications on observational cosmology, galaxies, and quasars; $20M in NASA/NSF grant support; eleven teaching awards; taught three online classes with 350,000+ students

speakerDetails.name: Joseph J. Kohn

speakerDetails.name: Tim Maudlin

speakerDetails.bio: B.A. in Physics and Philosophy (Yale); Ph.D. in History and Philosophy of Science (University of Pittsburgh); specializes in physical theory interpretation

speakerDetails.bio: Born July 26, 1957, St. Paul, Minnesota; B.S. Long Beach State (1980); M.S. San Diego State (1983); Ph.D. awarded 1988

title: A Freudian Perspective on What Ails the World Today
description: A colloquium jointly organized by The Helix Center for Interdisciplinary Investigation and L'Association Des Amis de Passages (ADAPes) Comite Freud. The event examined contemporary global crises through Freudian theory, focusing on identity formation, education, and religious/nationalist extremism. Per the organizers, "Freudian knowledge represents a return to reason, against the downward slide of identity crisis."

title: Art and Science: The Two Cultures Converging (3-Day Symposium)
description: A three-day symposium exploring convergences between artistic and scientific disciplines. Opening with an Einstein quote about how different disciplines create simplified models of the world, the event emphasized historical polymaths like Imhotep, Zhang Heng, Da Vinci, and Hildegard de Bingen as evidence of enduring art-science connections. The description notes: "from the drawing of star maps and anatomical sketches to the math and physics of optics and perspective, to the latest technological advances in computer design," demonstrating interdisciplinary dependence.

title: Science and the Big Questions (Series Overview)
description: The series comprises fourteen roundtables examining major scientific and philosophical inquiries. Topics include: "Knowledge and Limitations," "The Span of Infinity," "Complexity and Emergence," "The Search for Immortality," "The Sublime Experience," "The Meditative State," "The Realm of Mystery," "The Changing Nature of Free Will," "Genes, Computers, and Medicine," "Epigenetics at Work," "Speak, Memory," "Apprehending Consciousness," "Understanding Genius," and "The Mind of a Child."

title: Psychological Types Then and Now: The Relevance and Application of Jung's Theory
description: The event explored Jung's personality types theory as a flexible, four-function two-attitude model of introversion and extraversion. It examined how the Swiss psychiatrist developed this framework by contrasting his temperament with Freud and Adler. The description notes the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator's widespread use in couples and family therapy, vocational counseling, coaching, and organizational development, as well as psychoanalytic applications.

title: Synchronicity and Other Mind Matter Conjectures
description: The event explores the mind-matter relationship through the Pauli-Jung Conjecture. "How are mind and matter related? In the mid-20th century, the psychiatrist and analyst Carl Gustav Jung and the Nobel Laureate physicist Wolfgang Pauli formulated the concept of synchronicity." The discussion centers on dual-aspect monism, examining how the mental and the material are two complementary and intersecting aspects of one underlying reality.

title: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 1
description: The symposium explores Warburg's intellectual preoccupations including "memory, both in relation to different forms of artistic creation and in anticipation of concepts related to neuroplasticity and neuroesthetics." The program examines "the significance and fluency of the image -- its elliptical and metaphoric functions -- and of affect" alongside contemporary understanding of the unconscious and interdisciplinary thought.

title: Aby Warburg: Art, Neuroscience, and Psychoanalysis: Day 2
description: Continuation of the two-day symposium examining Warburg's concepts including memory in relation to artistic creation, neuroplasticity, and neuroesthetics. Focus areas include "the significance and fluency of the image -- its elliptical and metaphoric functions -- and of affect for the phenomena and qualia of chronology and memory, in concert with contemporary understanding of the dynamic unconscious; and the interdisciplinary mode of thought."
